rule:
**Er** says who you are and who someone else is — it is the present of **være**, to be, and it is the same for every person: **jeg er**, **du er**, **han er**.

A thing is **en** or **et**: **en mann**, **et barn**. You learn which with the word.

To say not, put **ikke** after the verb: **Jeg er ikke Tom.** For no, say **nei**.

The word for the is an ending, not a separate word: add **-en** to an en-word (**mann → mannen**) and **-et** to an et-word (**hus → huset**).

**Han** is he, **hun** is she. For a thing, **den** for an en-word, **det** for an et-word.

A job takes no article: **Han er lege.** **Hun er lærer.**

These are set phrases to learn whole.

**Takk** is thank you. **Vær så snill** is please; **vær så god** is here you are.

Greet with **god morgen**, **god dag**, **god kveld**; leave with **ha det**.

Ask **Hvordan går det?** and answer **Bra, takk.**

A verb in the present is one form for everyone: **jeg spiser**, **du spiser**, **han spiser**.

For liking, use **liker**: **Jeg liker kaffe.** **Liker du te?**

**Har** is have, and like other verbs it is one form: **jeg har**, **du har**, **han har**.

**Jeg har en hund.** **Har du en katt?**

Most nouns add **-er** to mean more than one: **hund → hunder**, **eple → epler**. Some et-words do not change: **et hus → to hus**.

We, you and they are **vi**, **dere**, **de**. The verb stays one form: **Vi er venner.**

An adjective adds **-t** with an et-word: **en fin bil**, but **et fint hus**.

**Veldig** is very, **også** is also: **Bilen er veldig fin.**

To say where something is, use **er**, or **står** for standing and **ligger** for lying: **Boka ligger på bordet.**

**i** in, **på** on, **under** under; **her** here, **der** there.

For there is, say **det er**: **Det er en katt i hagen.**

Say how you feel with **er** and an adjective: **Jeg er trøtt.** **Jeg er glad.**

Hungry, thirsty and cold are adjectives too: **Jeg er sulten.** **Jeg er tørst.** **Jeg er kald.**

To say whose, use **min** my, **din** your, **hans** his, **hennes** her, **vår** our: **Det er min bror.**

Family words: **far**, **mor**, **bror**, **søster**.

A question word comes first: **hvem** who, **hva** what, **hvor** where, **når** when, **hvorfor** why, **hvilken** which.

**Hvor er du?** To answer why, use **fordi**: **Fordi jeg er trøtt.**

The numbers one to ten: **én**, **to**, **tre**, **fire**, **fem**, **seks**, **sju**, **åtte**, **ni**, **ti**.

Ask how many with **hvor mange**. For an age, say the number and **år**: **Jeg er ti år.**

A color after **er** does not change: **Bilen er rød.**

Before a noun it adds **-t** with an et-word: **en rød bil**, **et rødt hus**.

**Farge** is color: **Hvilken farge?**

Time words: **i dag** today, **i morgen** tomorrow, **nå** now.

Days of the week take no capital: **mandag**, **lørdag**, **søndag**.

Ask the time with **Hva er klokka?**

**Går** is go, one form: **jeg går**, **du går**, **vi går**.

Use **til** for to a place: **Jeg går til skolen.** **Vi går til byen.**

To ask for help: **Jeg forstår ikke.** I don't understand.

**Saktere, takk.** Slower, please.

**En gang til.** One more time. **Gjenta, takk.** Repeat, please.

To ask about a word: **Hvordan sier du…?** How do you say…?

**Hva betyr…?** What does… mean?

**Ordet på norsk** the word in Norwegian; **på engelsk** in English.

When you can't find the word: **Jeg leter etter ordet…** I'm looking for the word…

**Det er en ting å…** It's a thing to…

**Jeg vet ikke.** I don't know. **Hva heter det?** What's it called?

To describe someone, use **har** for features: **Hun har blå øyne.**

An adjective adds **-t** with an et-word: **et kort ben**. **Han er pen.**

Say what you like doing with **liker å** and a verb: **Jeg liker å svømme.** **Jeg liker å danse.**

**Jeg liker musikk.** **Jeg liker fotball.**

Ask where with **Hvor er…?** The place takes the ending: **museet**, **kirka**, **stasjonen**.

For how you travel, use **med**: **med bussen**, **med toget**.

**nær** near, **langt** far.
